blocks.text: A different summary from the mean

The median is obtained from sorted values. We will use the usual convention: with an odd number of data points, it is the middle value; with an even number, it is the mean of the two middle values. The center is defined by positions in the sorted order, even when values are repeated. When repetitions occur, this does not mean there must be exactly as many strictly smaller values as strictly larger ones.

The arithmetic mean adds magnitudes; the median locates the center of a sorted collection. For {1, 2, 12}, the mean is five and the median is two. Neither summary automatically replaces the other: each answers a different question.

blocks.question: To find the median using this method, what preparation is needed?
options: Simply read the middle element in arrival order.
Sort the values or a copy of them.
Always add the values and divide by the size.
blocks.explanation: The middle position must belong to the order by value, not just any sequence.

blocks.text: The center of an odd number of values

For an odd, positive size, size() / 2 gives the middle index: with five elements, integer division yields two, leaving two positions on either side. Here integer division is intentional: we need an index, not a fractional measurement.

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: The sorted order is one, three, five, six, eight; the middle index two contains five.

blocks.question: In a sorted collection of three elements, which index is the middle one?
blocks.explanation: There is one position on either side of index one.

blocks.question: Fill in only the divisor digit that locates the middle index for any positive odd size, not only the three values in this example.
blocks.explanation: Integer division of the size by two gives the middle index for an odd size.

blocks.text: An even number of values has two middle positions

With four sorted elements, the middle indices are one and two. If centro = size() / 2, those indices are centro - 1 and centro. Choosing only datos[centro] gives the upper middle value, not the median under our convention. For {1, 4, 8, 9}, the median is six, even though that value does not appear in the collection.

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: The sorted middle values are four and six; their mean is five.

blocks.question: For the sorted data {2, 3, 8, 12}, which values contribute to the median?
options: Two and twelve.
Three and eight.
Only eight.
blocks.explanation: The two middle values occupy indices one and two.

blocks.text: We convert one value to double before adding them, so the addition in this expression is also performed in double. Dividing by 2.0 preserves the fractional part. We do not use an int sum that might overflow and expect a later conversion to repair it. In these exercises we use small quantities or measurements, not money that would require another representation.

First check that the collection is not empty. If the positive size is even, it is at least two, so centro is at least one and centro - 1 exists. If the size is odd, centro is always within bounds.

That all values are different.
That elements exist.
blocks.explanation: An empty collection has no middle positions and no median defined by this method.

blocks.question: The mean and median both came out to four in one example. What does this prove?
options: That sort did not run.
That they are always the same operation.
That they happened to agree in that case; other data may give different results.
blocks.explanation: Matching results do not erase the difference between their definitions.

blocks.text: Build a median for both count types

Build a general median calculation using a sorted copy. For {6, 1, 4}, display Median: 4. For {1, 6, 2, 9}, display Median: 4. For {}, display No data. Also check {5}, {2, 7}, {-5, -1}, {3, 3, 8}, and {4, 4, 4, 4}. Determine which branch applies and which indices will be used before running each test.
Keep a test table with the collection, resulting sorted order, size, middle indices, and expected median. This evidence justifies every access rather than merely showing that the program finished.
Reference solution preserving order and representing absence

blocks.question: Why is an even-sized collection with different middle values a necessary test?
options: Because odd-sized collections cannot be sorted.
Because it distinguishes the agreed-upon median from selecting only the upper middle value.
Because it forces you to modify the original values.
blocks.explanation: The test case must exercise the definition we intend to implement.

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.

blocks.question: What should your explanation say about the middle in the presence of duplicates?
options: That duplicates must be removed before calculating.
That it is defined by positions in the sorted collection, with the even-count convention made explicit.
That half the values must always be strictly smaller.
blocks.explanation: Removing repeated observations would change the data involved in the question.

blocks.text: Lab criteria: distinguish missing data, odd and even counts; justify the middle indices in value order; average both middle values while preserving fractions; do not remove repeated observations or modify the original.
